ext.title: Presidential Leadership and Legislative Polarization
ext.document_type: Working paper, formal theory (manuscript dated February 2024, 10,328 words). The text names no journal or publisher.
ext.identification: Not applicable: no estimation or causal identification. Claims are model-internal comparative statics. The authors call for future empirical work to test the predictions (p.5, p.25-26).
ext.coverage: Full text read: all 1613 lines of the extracted text, including title, abstract, introduction, related literature, model (Sec. 1), equilibrium (Sec. 2), dynamics (Sec. 3), electoral-strength extension (Sec. 4), conclusion (Sec. 5), references, and Online Appendix A.1-A.4. Page numbers cited are the manuscript's printed footers. All 118 of Paul's highlights were read from the single annotation file. The text does not discuss networks, lobbying, path-finding, allocation, or text measurement, and has no election data, so those topics are absent by design rather than skipped.
ext.research_question: How can presidential leadership, specifically going public, both raise issue salience to move Congress toward the president's policy and increase legislative polarization? And how does this tension shape a president's decision to go public in the first place? (p.1-2)
ext.theory: Going public raises issue salience and activates party bases, which pressure co-partisan and out-partisan legislators (Canes-Wrone 2006 versus Lee 2009's partisan retreat). The model combines pivotal-politics bargaining (Krehbiel 1998; Dziuda and Loeper 2018; Gehlbach 2021) with a partisan president whose reelection is tied to the policy outcome. Party branding and legislative-cartel logic (Cox and McCubbins 2005, 2007) motivates "defensive appeals," where the president goes public to deter co-partisan defection rather than to persuade out-partisans. Sincere polarization (z) and strategic polarization from base pressure (beta) and electoral stakes (delta) are manipulated separately (p.5-6, p.10-11).
ext.data: None. This is a formal model with no sample, unit, period, or N. Empirical material is limited to illustrations: Biden's 2023 debt-ceiling remarks (p.2), Biden's COVID emergency and abortion appeals (p.3, p.23), Trump's ACA repeal attempt (p.24), and a Pew 2019 poll showing a partisan gap of seven points on infrastructure versus 46 on health care (p.22). These are cited as illustrations, not tested.
ext.method: Game-theoretic model. Pure-strategy subgame perfect equilibrium solved by backward induction (p.11, p.13). Players are a president P, a left party L, a right party R, and a non-strategic challenger. The preference shock is theta ~ Uniform[-psi, psi]. Gridlock regions and cost thresholds for going public (c(1), c(-1)) are derived in closed form (Prop. 1-2, App. A.1-A.2). Comparative statics are reported as propositions (Prop. 3-5). Figures 1, 3, 4, and 5 give numerical illustrations at stated parameter values. Section 4 extends the model so the president's silent-reelection probability rho(x_sq) differs by status quo (Prop. 6, App. A.4).
ext.scope: Contemporary US presidency and two-party Congress with separation of powers, as motivated by 2021-2023 examples. The model covers one binary policy dimension, one issue, and two veto pivots (one per party). The president has no formal agenda power (p.4). The authors note the framework could also fit a mid-twentieth-century "golden age" of less polarized parties (p.23). Single-issue and single-dimension scope is stated as a limitation (p.31).

key_findings.finding: Going public always widens the gridlock region, even when both party bases rally behind the president. Silent gridlock region is (-z, z). Public gridlock region is bounded by (-z + beta_R - delta)/2 and (z + beta_L + delta)/2 (bar notation on beta lost in extraction). Asymmetric base influence drives this 'effective polarization.'
key_findings.location: Prop. 1 (p.13); Fig. 1 and note (p.14); proof in App. A.1 (p.38)
key_findings.numbers: Fig. 1 illustrative values: z = 1; beta_L > 0 = 0.75; beta_L < 0 = -0.5; beta_R > 0 = 0.5; beta_R < 0 = -0.75; delta = 0.5

key_findings.finding: Going public can raise presidential legislative success, not only polarization, because co-partisans move further toward the president than out-partisans under a Rally. This harmonizes Canes-Wrone (2006) with Lee (2009).

The president goes public for a wider range of opportunity costs when the status quo is favorable: c(-1) > c(1) always. Three regions result: c <= c(1) always goes public; c in (c(1), c(-1)] goes public only if status quo favorable; c > c(-1) never goes public.
key_findings.numbers: c(-1) - c(1) is shown to be positive for 0<p<1, 0<q<1, ps i > z > 0, delta > 0 (App. A.2, p.40)

key_findings.finding: Defensive appeal: under Partisan Retreat (q = 1), the president never goes public when the status quo is unfavorable (c_q(1) strictly negative), but always has an incentive to go public when the status quo is favorable (c_q(-1) strictly positive).

Under Backfire (1-p-q = 1), the president never goes public with an unfavorable status quo (c_b(1) = c_q(1)). With a favorable status quo she sometimes profits from going public even though it is certain to backfire. The threshold is beta_L < -delta(delta + 2z + 2) / (2(delta + 2)), which falls as z and delta rise.

Rally Around the President (p = 1): c_p(-1) and c_p(1) rise with the out-party base's support beta_R (for unfavorable status quo). The gap c_p(-1) - c_p(1) falls as beta_R rises. c_p(1) need not be positive, so the president may not go public even under the most favorable base reactions, because a high delta lets the out-party resist.

Prop. 3 (beliefs about reactions): c(1) increases in p; c(-1) increases in p and in q. Higher Backlash probability (1-p-q) reduces going public when the status quo is favorable. When unfavorable, Backlash or Retreat matters only if it comes at the expense of p.
key_findings.numbers: dc(1)/dp = (beta_R-bar - beta_R)(2+delta)/(2psi) > 0; dc(-1)/dq > 0 (sign as in proof)

key_findings.finding: Prop. 4 (legislative polarization z): going public becomes more likely with favorable status quo and less likely with unfavorable status quo as z rises.
key_findings.location: Prop. 4 (p.25); discussion of cross-sectional predictions (p.25-26); proof App. A.3.2 (p.42)
key_findings.numbers: dc(-1)/dz = delta/(2psi) > 0; dc(1)/dz = -delta/(2psi) < 0; d(Delta c)/dz = delta/psi > 0

key_findings.finding: Prop. 5 (policy uncertainty psi): the president is weakly less likely to go public as psi rises. The gap between favorable and unfavorable thresholds shrinks as psi rises, so the president's behavior is less sensitive to the status quo under high uncertainty.

Electoral strength extension: higher silent-reelection probability rho lowers the go-public range (Eqs. 12, 14). If rho(-1) > rho(1) and psi is large (psi > psi*, Eq. 15), the ordering of thresholds can flip so the president goes public more under an unfavorable status quo ('gambling for reelection', after Downs and Rocke 1994).

Illustrative empirical gap: Biden's 2021 infrastructure law fits the case of elite polarization exceeding mass polarization (z > 0, beta_R = beta_R-bar). The authors cite a Pew 2019 partisan gap of seven points on infrastructure versus 46 on health care. This is an illustration, not a test.
key_findings.numbers: partisan gap 7 points (infrastructure) vs 46 points (health care), Pew Research Center 2019

limitations: Stated by the authors: the election is blunt. The president wins or loses with certainty given the policy outcome, which ignores other electoral factors (p.30).
Stated: the model covers a single issue and a single dimension. Presidents strategically choose among issues and rhetorical arguments, which the model does not capture (p.30-31).
Stated: the model is policy-focused. A president may go public to signal commitment and mobilize a core constituency even when that dampens passage prospects (p.30).
Stated: the lack of party labels leaves open who the representative legislator and voter are (p.6). The two veto pivots are modeled as party representatives (fn. 4, p.8).
Stated: a Backfire is rarely observed, which may be endogenous to whether presidents raise salience on unpopular issues (p.24).
Stated: if z < psi, no preference shock could ever lead the parties to agree, so going public would never matter. The authors set this case aside (fn. 5, p.8).
Stated: the reelection probability after staying silent is fixed at 1/2 in the main model. Section 4 relaxes this (p.10, p.28).
Stated: the empirical implications (partisan gap, status quo, uncertainty) are not tested with data. The paper gives only illustrative examples.
Stated: several comparative statics hold only weakly, since cost thresholds can be negative and then parameter changes have no effect on behavior (fn. 10, p.18; App. A.3).
measures: Model primitives, not empirical measures: z (sincere/ideological polarization, common knowledge); psi (bound on preference shock, i.e., policy uncertainty); delta (reelection/co-partisan payoff); c (cost of going public); p, q, and 1-p-q (probabilities of Rally, Partisan Retreat, Backfire); beta_L and beta_R (party-base pressure, with upper and lower bounds); rho(x_sq) (silent-reelection probability). Status quo x_sq in {-1, 1}. Table 1 (p.8-9) gives the joint distribution of base reactions.
references_of_note: Canes-Wrone 2006, Who Leads Whom? Presidents, Policy, and the Public. The closest prior model: presidents go public when the representative voter is closer to them than the median lawmaker or status quo.
Lee 2009, Beyond Ideology. Presidential rhetoric pushes parties into partisan corners (partisan retreat); the main rival prediction.
Lee 2016 (no publisher given in the text beyond Chicago/London). Party branding and interbranch party competition for the White House.
Dziuda and Loeper 2018, Dynamic Pivotal Politics (APSR). The static pivotal-politics bargaining model the paper adapts.
Krehbiel 1998, Pivotal Politics. Veto-pivot framework underlying the model.
Gehlbach 2021, Formal Models of Domestic Politics. Source of the dynamic legislative bargaining model adapted in footnote 1.
Cox and McCubbins 2005 and 2007 (Setting the Agenda; Legislative Leviathan). Party cartel and branding logic behind defensive appeals.
Lebo and O'Geen 2011, The President's Role in the Partisan Congressional Arena. Presidents' reputations and the stylized fact that going-public presidents rise and fall with their policy.
Schnakenberg 2017, Informational lobbying and legislative voting (AJPS). Relevant to lobbying and information provision in legislatures.
Schnakenberg and Turner 2021, Helping friends or influencing foes: electoral and policy effects of campaign finance contributions (AJPS 65(1):88-100). Directly relevant to elections and influence.
Schnakenberg and Turner 2024, Formal Theories of Special Interest Influence (Annual Review of Political Science). Survey of formal lobbying theory.
Schnakenberg and Turner 2023, Political Influence and Dark Money (unpublished manuscript, SocArXiv 3bzex). Relevant to influence and electoral outcomes.
Ban, Park and You 2023, How Are Politicians Informed? Witnesses and Information Provision in Congress (APSR). Information and lobbying channels that shape preferences (theta).
Kriner and Schickler 2016, Investigating the President. Congressional oversight and information.
Downs and Rocke 1994, Gambling for Resurrection. Source of the 'gambling for reelection' logic in Sec. 4.
Howell, Jackman and Rogowski 2013, The Wartime President. Rally effects in national-security policy areas.
Howell, Porter and Wood 2020, Rethinking Public Appeals: experimental evidence on presidential performances. Experimental evidence on public appeals, relevant to persuasion.
Levendusky 2009, The Partisan Sort. Mass sorting, used to motivate low Rally probability.
Noble 2023, Presidential Cues and the Nationalization of Congressional Rhetoric, 1973-2016 (AJPS). Same author; empirical rhetoric and nationalization evidence.
Prato and Turner 2023, Institutional Foundations of the Power to Persuade (working paper, SocArXiv 4w9af). Companion persuasion work by co-author Turner.
Lowande 2021, Presidents and the Status Quo (QJPS). Status quo effects on presidential behavior.

rel.summary_md:
Noble and Turner build a formal model with no data. A partisan president decides whether to "go public" on one binary issue before two party pivots vote. Going public activates both party bases. The bases then rally, retreat (co-partisans move toward the president, out-partisans away) or backfire. It also ties the president's reelection to the outcome, which gives co-partisans an electoral stake (delta).

Results:
- Going public always widens the gridlock interval (Prop 1).
- Because the status quo matters, presidents go public over a wider range of costs when the status quo already favors them (c(-1) > c(1), Prop 2). The authors call this a "defensive appeal" aimed at fair-weather co-partisans.
- Under partisan retreat the president never goes public against an unfavorable status quo.
- Higher sincere polarization (z) makes going public more attractive in defense and less attractive on offense (Prop 4).
- Higher uncertainty (psi) weakly reduces going public and blunts its sensitivity to the status quo (Prop 5).
- The authors propose these as predictions to test. Nothing in the paper estimates them.

This matters because Melange implements the paper almost line for line in fec/engine/salience_shock.py and the dashboard's exec cue. The party asymmetry carries over faithfully. Several mappings do not. The estimator ties rally and retreat odds to the elite stance gap, psi is built from missing stance data, and the paper's presidential-reelection channel is moved onto legislators and onto a CU advocacy actor.

The sharpest problem is in the live advisory. It credits "defections prevented" on every issue, whatever its status quo, so its four GO PUBLIC verdicts (written 2026-10-08) all fall on offense issues. That reverses the paper's central prediction. This finding comes from one agent analysis path and stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: Going public is more attractive when the status quo is favorable: c(-1) > c(1) always (Prop 2). Under Partisan Retreat the president never goes public against an unfavorable status quo (c_q(1) < 0) but always has an incentive to defend a favorable one. The model predicts that going public occurs more often in defense of a favorable status quo than to win policy change (p.26). The defensive appeal logic depends on the co-partisan being the relevant pivot, which holds only when the status quo is favorable (p.17, p.24).
bearings.paper_location: Eqs. 7-8 and Prop. 2 (p.16-17); Partisan Retreat (p.22-23); p.26; App. A.2 (p.39-40)
bearings.system_side: defensive_appeal_value() runs for every issue with no status-quo check. The advisory value is E_dspread + 1.5 x len(defections_prevented) for offense and defend issues alike. In the live salience_advisory.json (2026-10-08 15:37, 18 issues), the four GO PUBLIC verdicts (top quartile, cut 68.27) are all sq=offense, and each is driven by held counts: Technology & Emerging (E_dspread -3.87, held 67, q=0.83), Member Business Lending (+5.83, held 60), Data Privacy (-19.35, held 68) and Fraud Prevention (-9.73, held 52). The three defend issues rank 13th to 15th. Tech & Emerging is close to the paper's pure-retreat case on an unfavorable status quo, where the paper says never go public, yet it is ranked first. The dashboard bundle surfaces these verdicts as 'GO PUBLIC · holds N'. UNVERIFIED single-path analysis (DE-062).
bearings.transfer_conditions: No empirical transfer is needed. This is an internal-consistency check against the model the code claims to implement. The contradiction holds whenever the defensive credit is added on sq='offense' issues. Gating held to sq=='defend' would restore the paper's ordering. Whether the paper's ordering is right for a CU advocacy campaign is a separate, untested question.

bearings.paper_claim: Sincere legislative polarization z and base-pressure reactions (beta_L, beta_R, with probabilities p, q, 1-p-q) are separate primitives that the authors vary independently. The infrastructure illustration (Pew 2019 partisan gap of 7 points vs 46 on health care) is presented as a case where elite polarization exceeds mass polarization and a Rally is still possible.
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 1 and Table 1 (p.8-9); Prop. 3 Rally discussion (p.22); Prop. 4 (p.25)
bearings.system_side: salience_issue_params estimates z as the absolute D-R gap in mean legislator stance tier. It then sets q = (1-b) x min(1, z/3) and p = (1-b)(1 - z/3). The elite stance gap therefore sets the mass-base reaction odds. The resulting regime mixture drives both the advisory and the dashboard exec cue.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The mapping is a design choice, not something the paper implies. It holds only if base reactions on CU issues track legislator stance gaps. That would need a base-side or mass-opinion measure, such as a partisan gap in public or credit-union-member opinion per issue, which the system does not have. The paper's own example warns that the two can diverge.

bearings.paper_claim: psi bounds a common preference shock and stands for informational policy uncertainty. Higher psi makes the president weakly less likely to go public and shrinks the favorable-vs-unfavorable gap (Prop 5). The paper never links psi to the probability of Backfire. Under a favorable status quo, going public can pay even when backfire is certain (the threshold on beta_L falls as z and delta rise).
bearings.system_side: psi = 1 - (share of members with a stance tier) + 0.3 x (True-Neutral share). This measures missing posture data, not uncertainty about preferences. Backfire is b = min(0.35, 0.05 + 0.10 psi), labelled 'Prop 5 caution'. The actual Prop 5 effect (damping go-public value) sits behind SAL_PSI_DAMP, which defaults to 0, so it appears only as a text tag at psi >= 0.8. Backfire steps are always non-positive, so the favorable-status-quo case where backfire still pays is not represented.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Data missingness stands in for psi only if a member's lack of a stance label reflects real preference uncertainty rather than collection gaps. Coverage is known to differ by party and chamber (press collector). The b-psi link has no support in this paper and should be cited as a design prior.

bearings.paper_claim: Section 4 lets the president's silent-reelection probability rho(x_sq) vary. A higher rho lowers the go-public range. When rho(-1) > rho(1) and psi > psi*, the president may 'gamble for reelection' by going public on an unfavorable status quo (Prop 6, Eq. 15). Legislators' delta is their stake in their party winning the White House, not in their own seats.
bearings.system_side: VULN multiplies every legislator's salience step by 1.35 if the member has a defend or contest electoral play, with the comment 'Noble A.4: gambling for reelection'. In backfire, co-partisans with a live race are held at 0 ('delta dominates base: Sec 3.1').
bearings.transfer_conditions: This paper does not support the amplifier. Its rho and the gambling logic concern the actor who goes public (the president), not the responsiveness of rank-and-file legislators. Any support for 'electorally vulnerable members respond more' has to come from elsewhere (for example, the electoral-incentives literature), and the 1.35 constant is uncalibrated.

bearings.paper_claim: There are three base-reaction regimes: Rally (both toward), Partisan Retreat (co toward, out away) and Backfire (both away, out more). The single restriction is beta_L > beta_R: co-partisans always favor the president's proposal more than out-partisans do. Going public adds the electoral stake delta to the thresholds as (z + beta_L + delta)/2 and (-z + beta_R - delta)/2.
bearings.system_side: steps_for() keeps the co-partisan step above the out-partisan step in all three regimes. Rally is co +1, out +0.5 only if bpf >= 0.30. Retreat is co +1, out -1. Backfire is co 0 or -0.5, out -1. The dashboard exec cue (EXECP='R') applies the same p, q, b mixture to bystander mobilization. The defensive channel instead scales the money-defection threshold multiplicatively, by DTHRESH x (1 + DELTA/2) with DELTA = 0.5. The actor is generalized from the president to a CU-side campaign whose party is set by --party.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The regime structure transfers most cleanly to the dashboard's executive cue, which matches the paper's presidential actor in a federal two-party Congress. It transfers less well to an ACU or industry 'going public' actor, which has no reelection tied to the outcome. The delta channel exists only because co-partisans share the president's electoral fate. The bpf >= 0.30 cutoff, the step sizes and the multiplicative delta are the code's own design, not the paper's. The paper's delta is additive in the vote threshold and has no money-defection analog.

bearings.paper_claim: 'Gridlock region' means the range of the common preference shock theta over which two pivots keep the status quo. Going public always widens it, even under a Rally, because asymmetric base pressure creates 'effective polarization'.
bearings.system_side: gridlock_width counts members whose tier sits in a five-rung MIDBAND, and E_dmidband reports its change. The comments read a falling count as 'Prop 1 hollowing' and a rising count on defend issues as a win. The count is reported but not used in the verdict.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Occupancy of a middle band among 533 members is a different quantity from a shock interval between two pivots. Prop 1 makes no prediction about its sign, so the metric cannot be read as testing or reproducing Prop 1.

gaps_exposed: The status quo does not gate the defensive-appeal credit. The paper confines defensive appeals to a favorable status quo, but the advisory adds 1.5 x defections_prevented on offense issues too, and its top-quartile GO PUBLIC verdicts follow from that.
No base-side or mass-opinion measure per issue. The paper separates elite polarization z from base reactions p, q and beta, but the system derives both from the legislator stance matrix.

The Prop 4 interaction between z and the status quo is not modeled. Higher z should favor going public on defend issues and disfavor it on offense issues, but the system has no z-by-status-quo term beyond retreat odds.
The Prop 5 uncertainty damping is off by default (SAL_PSI_DAMP = 0), and psi is measured as missing stance data, not as preference-shock uncertainty.
The actor's own electoral stake (rho or delta for the campaigning actor) and an opportunity cost c per issue are absent. The opportunity cost is replaced by a fixed top-quartile cut.
There is no favorable-status-quo case in which going public pays despite a certain backfire, because backfire steps are always non-positive.

There is no prospective test of any going-public prediction. For example: after a CU-side public campaign, did co-partisans shift more than out-partisans, and did retreat-regime issues polarize further? The paper explicitly calls for such empirical tests.
flags: UNVERIFIED (DE-062): the finding that the live salience_advisory.json ranks only offense issues GO PUBLIC because of the defensive-held credit comes from one agent read of the 2026-10-08 file and code. A second path should reproduce it before anyone acts on it.

The advisory's 'GO PUBLIC · holds N' verdict reaches the dashboard (build_dashboard_bundle.py:677-682). Under the code's own Noble framing, it currently points the CU shop toward going loud on the issues where the paper says quiet work dominates.
The VULN x1.35 amplifier and b = 0.05 + 0.10 psi are labelled in code comments as Noble A.4 and Prop 5. This paper supports neither, so both should be cited as design priors.

Model outputs here (E_dspread, defections_prevented, p, q and b per issue) are heuristic outputs of a formal model with no data. They are not probabilities of real-world rally or retreat, and each figure should name its window (the current stance matrix) and its denominator (533 members, or the members with a tier on that issue).
No conflict with D-021 (LDA), the two rejected SNA proposals or reciprocity (D-104..D-108). The paper does not touch networks or lobbying data.
rel.paul_alignment: Paul highlighted the paper heavily but wrote no annotation. Both annotation files hold only the bibliography, with no takeaways. His highlights concentrate on the regimes (rally, retreat, backfire), defensive appeals, status-quo dependence and uncertainty. They include "going public is unlikely to help her" under an unfavorable status quo (p.4), "presidents always have an incentive to go public when the status quo is favorable" (p.23) and the p.26 prediction about defending a favorable status quo. They also include "less likely to go public on new or volatile policy areas" (p.27-28). The system adopted the regime structure he marked. However, the live advisory runs against the status-quo highlights: all four GO PUBLIC issues are offense issues, and Technology & Emerging is the most retreat-prone of them. The uncertainty highlights appear only as a text caution, because the PSI_DAMP dial defaults to 0. His notes are not stale so much as empty. The component cites the paper as its basis, but the paper's own status-quo logic is applied inconsistently in the verdict.

related.why: Merkley and Stecula give empirical evidence of out-party backlash to elite party cues (Republican backlash on climate). That is the Backfire or Retreat regime Noble and Turner model only in theory, and it is cited alongside them in the salience-shock component.

Bakker et al. test why partisans accept co-partisan cues and reject out-party cues. That is the micro-foundation for Noble and Turner's assumed beta_L > beta_R, which the system's steps_for and cpf_pressure both encode.

Fouirnaies and Hall supply the empirical support (state legislators' effort responds to electoral incentives) that the VULN x1.35 amplifier needs and that Noble and Turner's Sec. 4 does not provide. Their evidence comes from state legislatures, so it bears on but does not settle federal salience response.

Linde and Vis give experimental evidence on politicians' risk-taking in the loss domain. That is a behavioral basis for the 'gambling for reelection' logic Noble and Turner borrow from Downs and Rocke, but it applies to legislators rather than to the president who goes public.

NOMINATE offers a roll-call measure of elite ideological polarization. It is an alternative, independent estimate of z to the system's stance-tier D-R gap, and it is separate from the base-reaction odds the system derives from that same gap.
